note: Navigation-accuracy baseline (#328). Regenerate with `UPDATE_PERF_BASELINE=1 cargo test -p strapdown-core --test perf_baseline`, then review the diff: every changed number is a claim about the navigation solution. Values are rounded to 6 significant figures. `null` means the metric is not computable for that scenario -- dead reckoning reports no covariance -- and is not gated. `"gated": false` keeps a metric recorded but unasserted. See the module docs in core/tests/perf_baseline.rs for what the numbers do and do not measure.

containment_3sigma_horizontal.note: 0.494, down from an unfalsifiable 1.000; see the UKF row. The EKF applied the absolute floor in both predict and update, so its fabricated sigma was 493 m.

npes_position.note: Not the horizontal channel: containment reads a flat 1.000 there, so each horizontal term is bounded by 9. Almost all of this is the vertical channel, whose containment is 0.41. real_rbpf_slice__rbpf.description: first 1200 records of test_data.csv, GNSS every epoch, 500 particles

horizontal_cep95_m.note: Not gated: this row's tail statistics are platform-dependent, because the tail IS the handful of epochs where the particle cloud collapses (#385). Measured on the same commit, Linux 34.02 m against Windows 24.33 m -- a 28.5% spread, wider than the improve band, so a Linux bless fails the Windows leg. The bulk statistics on this row agree across platforms to about 1% (horizontal_rmse_m +1.3%, containment_3sigma_horizontal +0.8%) and stay gated. horizontal_max_m is the same kind of statistic and currently sits at +4.7%, inside the band; it is worth watching rather than pre-emptively ungating. Re-gate this when #385 lands. Note also that the baseline is blessed on one platform and gated on three, with no cross-platform tolerance anywhere in judge() -- see #386.

npes_position.note: Not gated: dominated by an RBPF covariance collapse, not by navigation accuracy. 17 of 1,200 epochs report a horizontal sigma below 1 mm -- the smallest is 4.2 nm -- so this mean of e^2/P is set by a near-zero denominator on ~1.4% of rows. Exposed rather than caused by #367: before it, every row was sampled one IMU step late, after `predict` had re-inflated the cloud, which hid the collapse and recorded 183.5 here. Tracked in #385. `containment_3sigma_horizontal` on this row is unaffected and stays gated.

syn_cruise_1hz__ekf.description: synthetic 300 s at 50 Hz, GNSS every 1 s, scored against exact truth

npes_position.note: Up under #374, while every accuracy metric on the same row improved substantially (vertical RMSE ~0.83 to ~0.48 m, roll and pitch by 2-3x). Both directions are the same mechanism: this scenario runs at 50 Hz and was receiving 50x the intended process noise, so its covariance was inflated. Removing that improves the estimate and tightens the covariance, and a tighter covariance under an unchanged error is a larger normalised error. The consistency gap this exposes is #372's and #373's to close; it was previously hidden by the inflation.

roll_rmse_deg.note: 0.96 deg, up from 0.12 before #373, and pitch with it. Same cause as the UKF's yaw row: with the fabricated 201 m horizontal sigma gone, position is no longer pinned to the fix, so attitude error is no longer absorbed there and is measured for the first time. Under a degree in absolute terms and the best of the three. Tracked with #372/#373's consistency work.

vertical_rmse_m.note: About a quarter worse than at the old 1e-4 altitude process noise, and the stated price of that retune: the old value bought this RMSE by reporting an uncertainty roughly half the actual error. Containment in the same row moved 0.88 -> 0.93 toward 0.9973. On the reference recording vertical RMSE did not pay this price at all -- it improved slightly. See VERTICAL_POSITION_PROCESS_NOISE_M2 in core/src/sim.rs.

yaw_rmse_deg.note: 89.79 deg, up from 42.66 before #373 -- and this row has no magnetometer, so yaw is observable only through the GNSS velocity fix. The EKF reaches 1.33 deg on the identical stream. The regression is not a tuning loss: removing the absolute 1e-9 covariance floor stopped this filter pinning its position to each fix, and what had been masking the sigma-point attitude defect was exactly that pinning. Swept over alpha at 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 0.5 and 1.0, yaw reads 89.8, 90.5, 90.1, 96.5 and 108.3 deg -- so widening the sigma-point spread makes it worse and the tiny `n + lambda` scaling is NOT the cause. That refutes the conditioning hypothesis and leaves #371's original diagnosis, the linear Euler mean over sigma-point attitudes, as the live one.

npes_position.note: `sim::dead_reckoning` emits no covariance, so the three consistency metrics are `null` here. This scenario is what exercises that path end to end.

syn_outage_60s__ukf.description: synthetic 300 s at 50 Hz, 60 s of GNSS then 60 s of outage

horizontal_cep95_m.note: Worse after the vertical process-noise retune (was 221.67 m / 412.96 m / 13.62 m/s / 0.59 m/s / 3.51 deg at the old 1e-4). Recorded, not endorsed. This row does not respond monotonically to that knob -- across a four-decade sweep the horizontal RMSE runs 222, 174, 267, 344 m while the yaw error runs 105, 98, 21, 34 deg, so position gets worse exactly where attitude gets five times better. That is #371 -- a linear Euler mean over sigma-point attitudes -- coasting a 60 s GNSS outage, and it bounces under any perturbation. Read `syn_outage_60s__eskf`, which is monotone, for what the retune did.

horizontal_max_m.note: As `real_outage_60s__eskf`: a single sample at the end of a coast.

horizontal_rmse_m.note: 858 m, up from 251. A 60 s free-inertial coast is where process noise matters most, and #374 cut what this 50 Hz scenario receives by 50x -- it had been given a full second of random walk every 20 ms. With an honest Q the filter is far more confident through the coast, so the attitude error it coasts on is no longer masked by an inflated covariance. The ESKF's equivalent row *improved* over the same change, 20.07 m to 12.17 m, which is what a filter with sound attitude does here. The difference between them is #371: this row's yaw went 24.8 to 95.2 deg while the ESKF's stayed near 1 deg.

yaw_rmse_deg.note: 95.2 deg, up from 24.8. Same cause as the horizontal row above and as this scenario's sibling at `syn_cruise_1hz__ukf`: #371's linear Euler mean over sigma-point attitudes, now unmasked twice over -- once by #373 removing the covariance floor that pinned position, and again by #374 removing 50x of process noise that was hiding the drift. Uniformly random yaw would be about 104 deg RMS, so this filter has essentially no heading through the coast.
